title: Elif Shafak: Fiction is not a luxury. It’s existential
gist: Interview with novelist Elif Shafak, who left Turkey for London in 2008 after being tried for 'offending Turkishness' and facing state investigations, and now considers London home amid Erdoğan's tightening grip on universities, media and the judiciary. She argues fiction is existential in dark times, and that news avoidance and apathy, more than pessimism, feed polarisation and authoritarianism.

themes.theme: State repression of writers in Turkey

insights.claim: Shafak was tried in 2006 for 'offending Turkishness' after her novel The Bastard of Istanbul discussed the 1915-16 Armenian genocide; the prosecutor sought three years in prison, she was acquitted on all charges but needed a bodyguard for a year and a half.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Illustrates long-running Turkish legal risk around free expression — a governance risk factor.
insights.quote: I was put on trial, accused of ‘offending Turkishness’. The prosecutor asked for three years in prison.
insights.locator: I joke that the last thing

insights.claim: In 2019 Turkish police investigated her novels The Gaze and 10 Minutes 38 Seconds in This Strange World for alleged obscenity; she was again vindicated, and says Turkish writers live under a sword of Damocles of investigation, prosecution, exile or imprisonment.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Ongoing legal intimidation of cultural figures signals weak rule of law in Turkey.
insights.quote: As a Turkish writer, it’s almost like the sword of Damocles is hanging over you

insights.claim: Shafak says President Erdoğan's regime has tightened its grip on Turkey's universities, media and judiciary, restricting dissent and pressuring artists, women's rights groups and the LGBTQ+ community; she says Turkey deserves a functioning liberal democracy.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Institutional erosion in Turkey underpins political-risk premia on Turkish assets.
insights.quote: it deserves a proper, functioning, liberal democracy
insights.locator: With a PhD in political science

insights.claim: Shafak expects never to live in Turkey again because the repressive atmosphere that drove her out appears to be worsening, though her books are still widely read there.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Indicates no expected liberalisation trend in Turkey from an informed insider view.

insights.claim: Shafak moved to London with her children in 2008, citing the government's clampdown on journalists, intellectuals and artists and online abuse after coming out as bisexual in a TED talk; she chose 'permanent self-exile' to write about the 'silences' of official history.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Example of talent and intellectual flight from Turkey to the UK.
insights.quote: For that, I had to send myself permanently into self-exile.
insights.locator: In 2008, Shafak and her two children

insights.claim: Shafak, appointed president of the Royal Society of Literature in 2025 succeeding Bernardine Evaristo, champions 'multiple belongings' and London's multicultural schooling as a cultural enrichment.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Positive case for London's cosmopolitan pull on global talent.
insights.locator: Shafak has now lived in London

insights.claim: Shafak's new novel In One Brief Moment All Eternity (Viking) fictionalises Gustave Flaubert, tried in 1857 over Madame Bovary and acquitted, with the trial's publicity helping make the book famous; it is told by women including Emma Bovary.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Censorship attempts can backfire and amplify the work — a Streisand-effect precedent.

insights.claim: After a depression that began around 2024 amid Ukraine, the destruction of Gaza and Sudan, Shafak concluded fiction is not a luxury but existential, noting Flaubert wrote Madame Bovary while the world was falling apart.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Cultural demand for meaning-making narratives rises in crisis periods.
insights.quote: I never believe fiction is a luxury—I believe it’s existential.
insights.locator: The book was borne out of

insights.claim: If literature had no power, governments wouldn't bother suppressing voices; Shafak says humans are storytelling animals whose need for stories deepens in times of crisis.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Narrative control is a lever authoritarian states actively contest.
insights.locator: Perhaps if literature had no power

insights.claim: Shafak argues 24/7 news and social media deliver too much information, too little knowledge and even less wisdom, leaving people anxious and tired.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Information fatigue shapes media consumption and engagement patterns.
insights.quote: too much information, too little knowledge, and even less wisdom

insights.claim: Many people in the UK now say they no longer read the news because it is too demoralising; Shafak warns that retreat from public space lets extreme views dominate, and that every country with rising authoritarianism has seen extreme polarisation which autocrats exploit.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: News avoidance is a leading indicator of polarisation and democratic backsliding risk.
insights.quote: What scares me is not pessimism; what scares me is apathy.

insights.claim: Shafak contends organised religions divide humanity into 'us' versus 'them', while learning comes from exposure to difference rather than sameness, as she wrote in How to Stay Sane in an Age of Division (2020).
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
entities: How to Stay Sane in an Age of Division
insights.so_what: Frames polarisation as an identity-sorting dynamic that cross-cutting connections can counter.
insights.quote: The moment we stop listening to diverse opinions is also when we stop learning.

insights.claim: Shafak proposes human-to-human connection across borders and tribes as the answer to numbing isolation, with literature as an antidote to apathy because it builds empathy.
insights.speaker: Graeme Green
insights.so_what: Soft-power and cultural sectors claim a role in social cohesion.
insights.quote: literature is the antidote to apathy
